Chastening
CHAY-suh-ning
n.
From Latin castigare, “to correct, purify,” from castus (pure) + agere (to drive); rendering the Greek paideia, “the training and discipline of a child.”

See also: Chastening

📖 Biblical Definition

Chastening is the fatherly discipline by which God corrects, trains, and purifies His children through affliction, for their good and their growth in holiness—an exercise not of His wrath but of His love. The great passage is Hebrews 12, which applies the proverb: ‘My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.’ The Greek word, paideia, denotes the whole training and discipline of a child by a wise father—including instruction, correction, and, when needed, the rod—and this is precisely how God deals with His sons. Several truths are essential. First, chastening is a mark of sonship, not of rejection: ‘if ye be without chastisement... then are ye bastards, and not sons.’ The very afflictions that the unbelieving might take as signs of God’s anger are, to the believer, proofs of the Father’s love and tokens of his adoption. Second, chastening is wholly distinct from condemnation: Christ has borne the believer’s penalty, so that God’s dealings with His children are never punitive in the sense of satisfying justice—that was satisfied at the cross—but corrective and educative, aimed at their profit. Third, its purpose is holiness: earthly fathers chasten as seems good to them, ‘but he for our profit, that we might be partakers of his holiness’; the painful pruning is that the branch may bring forth more fruit. Chastening may take many forms—sickness, loss, disappointment, the bitter consequences of one’s own sins, or trials sent without any particular sin in view—and it is, for the present, not joyous but grievous; nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby. The right response to chastening is neither to despise it (making light of God’s hand, hardening oneself, learning nothing) nor to faint under it (sinking into despair, as though God had cast one off), but to be ‘exercised’ by it—humbling oneself, examining one’s ways, submitting to the Father’s wise and loving purpose, and so reaping the harvest of holiness it is designed to yield.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CHASTEN as to correct by punishment; to afflict by way of correction; to discipline; especially, the fatherly correction God administers to His people.

expand to see more

CHASTEN, v.t. — 1. To correct by punishment; to punish; to inflict pain for the purpose of reclaiming an offender; as, to chasten a son with a rod. 2. To afflict by other means... designed to call men from sin, and to subject their passions to the divine will.

CHASTISEMENT, n. — Correction; punishment; pain inflicted for punishment and correction, either by stripes or otherwise.

📖 Key Scripture

Hebrews 12:6 — "For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth."

Hebrews 12:10-11 — "...but he for our profit, that we might be partakers of his holiness. Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby."

Revelation 3:19 — "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent."

Psalm 119:71 — "It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Chastening is corrupted by reading all affliction as God’s punitive wrath (denying the cross has borne the believer’s penalty), and oppositely by the prosperity teaching that treats all suffering as defeat rather than a Father’s loving discipline.

expand to see more

Chastening is corrupted first by the failure to distinguish it from condemnation—the mistaken reading of every affliction as a sign of God’s punitive wrath against the believer. This drives the tender conscience to despair, supposing that each trial is the stroke of an angry Judge, and it denies the finished work of the cross, where the believer’s penalty was fully borne by Christ. God’s dealings with His justified children are never punitive in the sense of satisfying justice—that is forever settled—but always fatherly: corrective, educative, and loving, the discipline of a wise Father training His sons, not the sentence of a Judge condemning the guilty. To confuse the rod of a loving Father with the sword of an offended Judge is to misread God’s heart toward His people.

The opposite corruption, native to the prosperity gospel and the comfort-loving age, treats all suffering as defeat, failure, or the absence of God’s favor—something to be escaped, rebuked, or claimed away, never received as a Father’s loving discipline. But Scripture says the very opposite: chastening is a mark of sonship, and the absence of it would prove one a bastard and not a son; whom the Lord loves He chastens. To resent or flee all affliction is to despise the chastening of the Lord and to forfeit its fruit. The biblical doctrine steers between despair and resentment: chastening is the fatherly discipline of a loving God, distinct from condemnation, aimed at the believer’s profit and holiness, painful for the present but yielding afterward the peaceable fruit of righteousness. The right response is to be ‘exercised’ by it—neither despising the rod by hardening oneself nor fainting under it by sinking into despair, but humbling oneself, examining one’s ways, submitting to the Father’s wise purpose, and so reaping the harvest of holiness for which the discipline was sent. It is good for the believer that he has been afflicted, that he might learn God’s statutes.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The doctrine rests on paideia (the training and discipline of a son) by a Father who chastens whom He loves (agapaō), for partaking of His holiness.

Usage

"Chastening is the Father’s loving discipline of His sons—corrective, not condemning; a mark of sonship, not wrath."

"‘Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth’—the absence of discipline would prove one a bastard, not a son."

"The right response to chastening is to be exercised by it—neither despising the rod nor fainting under it."
